{"summary":"Extensive research shows that vaccines do not cause autism and there is no credible scientific evidence supporting a link between vaccines, their ingredients, and autism spectrum disorder (ASD).chop+2​
Scientific Evidence


Multiple large-scale studies, including those by the CDC and the Institute of Medicine, have confirmed that children who receive vaccines are not more likely to develop autism than those who do not.cdc+1​


The theory linking the MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccine to autism was based on a 1998 study that was later retracted due to scientific misconduct and data fraud; the lead author lost his medical license.kidshealth+1​


Nine CDC-funded studies since 2003 found no link between thimerosal (a mercury-based preservative) in vaccines and ASD.cdc​


Misinformation and Public Health


Despite persistent myths, experts and major health organizations universally agree there is no connection between vaccines and autism.chop+2​


Avoiding vaccines is risky, exposing children to preventable diseases with real potential for severe illness and death.kidshealth​


Conclusion
Vaccines are safe, do not cause autism, and remain a critical tool for preventing serious diseases. Claims to the contrary are not supported by scientific data.chop+2​","citations":["https://www.chop.edu/vaccine-education-center/vaccine-safety/vaccines-and-other-conditions/autism","https://www.cdc.gov/vaccine-safety/about/autism.html","https://kidshealth.org/en/parents/autism-studies.html"],"extractionConfidence":1,"extractionWarnings":[]}
